messages.subject: Studentships: National Centre for Statistical Ecology
messages.subject_clean: Studentships: National Centre for Statistical Ecology
messages.body_plain:
_________________________________________

           N A T I O N A L   C E N T R E   F O R

           S T A T I S T I C A L   E C O L O G Y
         _________________________________________

The National Centre for Statistical Ecology (NCSE) is a new joint venture
between the Universities of Cambridge, Kent and St Andrews, funded under
the EPSRC multidisciplinary critical mass in Mathematics initiative.  It
links the research groups in statistical ecology at the three
Universities.  Over the next few years, there will be a number of research
positions at the Centre, for research students and post-docs.

We are currently seeking gifted students in statistics or mathematics who
are highly motivated to apply their skills to postgraduate research in
statistical ecology.

The following five PhD studentships are currently available.  Each student
will be a member of NCSE, and will spend time at each of Cambridge, Kent
and St Andrews.  Projects 1 and 5 will be based primarily at Cambridge,
project 3 primarily at Kent, and projects 2 and 4 primarily at St
Andrews.  Projects 1-4 are open to all students, but for students from
outside the EU, there is no guarantee that the cost of fees will be fully
met.  Projects 1-3 and 5 have enhanced stipends; the stipend for project 4
is set at the EPSRC norm (12000 pounds in 2005-06).  Note that the topic
of project 4 is open, and proposals for distance sampling projects will be
welcome.

1. Integrated modelling of bird populations

Supervisors:  Steve Brooks (Cambridge) and Steve Freeman (British Trust
for Ornithology)

This project aims to develop Bayesian statistical methodology to underpin
and improve advice given to government and other bodies on the state of
the UK bird populations.  Markov chain Monte Carlo methods will be used to
fit comprehensive modelling structures to the data, which combine all
sources of relevant information to fully describe the complex underlying
population dynamics and their interaction with human activity and the
environment.

2. Population regulation in a changing world: common guillemots in Britain
and Ireland

Supervisors: Morten Frederiksen & Sarah Wanless (Centre for Ecology and
Hydrology, Banchory), and Steve Buckland & John Harwood (St Andrews)

This project will investigate the mechanisms leading to apparent
population regulation in common guillemots, and how these might be
affected by environmental change.  Data on breeding success from 11
colonies will be used together with data on adult survival and recruitment
from the long-term studies at the Isle of May, Canna and
Colonsay.  Population models will be used to investigate whether observed
changes in parameters are sufficient to regulate population size.

3. Climate modelling for prediction

Supervisors: Byron Morgan (Kent) and Ian Jolliffe (Reading)

Models will be developed for quantifying climate effects on animal
populations.  This will involve modelling appropriate climate
indices.  Long-term data sets for testing the methods will be available
for red deer, soay sheep and bighorn sheep.  A focus of the project will
be the development of systematic approaches, applicable to a wide range of
ecological examples.

4. The St Andrews Studentship in Statistical Ecology

The subject of research can be any topic from statistical ecology in which
there is current research interest at St Andrews.  Two areas of particular
strength are modelling population dynamics and distance sampling, but
other research topics are also possible.  Candidates can submit their own
proposal if they wish;  otherwise, potential projects will be offered.

5. A Mathematical Model of Circadian Signalling

Supervisors: Alex Webb, Jorge Concales & Steve Brooks (Cambridge) and
Andrew Millar (Edinburgh)

This project aims to model the circadian regulation of the Ca2+ signalling
network in Arabidopsis. This will provide a mathematical model of a
sub-cellular signalling network, which is a central step towards an
integrated model of plant cell biology. You will develop a deterministic
model for the role of Ca2+ and other signalling intermediates in the plant
circadian signalling network based on ordinary differential equations
(ODE). You will integrate it with the Millar model of the central
oscillator. This will produce the first mathematical model of the
circadian regulation signalling molecules in the plant.

Negotiations are currently taking place which may result in a further
studentship, involving collaboration between Kent and the Max Planck
Institute in Rostock in Germany, for work in evolutionary bio-demography,
and joint supervision by Dr. David Thomson.

More details of NCSE and of the projects are given at
http://www.ncse.org.uk/
You may also contact the Centre Director Byron Morgan
(B.J.T....@kent.ac.uk) or Co-directors Steve Brooks
(S.P.B...@statslab.cam.ac.uk) and Steve Buckland
(st...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk) directly.  Application forms can be obtained from
Byron Morgan.  Applications by 16th April please;  early applications may
be favoured.

messages.subject: Re: choosing cut points
messages.body_plain:
> > I have a question concerning the choice of cutpoints when grouping data.
> >
> > is it better to choose rounded cutpoints values (i e 10 m, 20m 30m ..) or

> > to choose a fixed number of intervals, with decimal values of cutpoints ?.
> > we have an example for wich with the same number of intervals, and the same

> > function, the GOF test and the CV are better in the second case.
> > visually, the adjustment curves seems similar..
> >

> > I think I do not have heaping problem, as rangefinders (precision 1m) were used

If you don't have a problem with heaping, then you're really only choosing
cutpoints for visual presentation of the data and model fits.  Distance 4
has goodness-of-fit tests that don't require you to group the data
(Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises).  I would use those, in which
case choice of intervals isn't important.  (If there were heaping, I would
choose cutpoints well away from the distances at which observations are
heaped.)

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: EDR
messages.body_plain:
> > Are effective detection radii affected by left-truncation?  In my case,
> > I truncated all detections within 12.5 m - based on examinations of
> > distance vs. frequency histograms.

They are not in the sense that, if you had perfect data, left-truncation
would still give the same estimate of effective detection radius on
average.  However, you need to be very clear on what is causing a problem
with your data, before deciding whether left-truncation is appropriate.

Left-truncation is more commonly used for line transect sampling, e.g. in
aerial surveys where it becomes apparent that some animals close to the
line are being missed.  In point-transect sampling, you might for example
get songbirds in dense cover that stop singing when you are very near,
causing you to miss them.  Or birds near the point may flee undetected,
beyond the range of detection, leaving a 'hole' around the point.
Left-truncation might help in either case.  However, if birds move a
little away from the point, so that you get too few detections near the
point but too many at middle distances, left-truncation will cause you to
overestimate density;  better then not to truncate, so that the excess at
mid-distances tends to average out with the shortage near the point.
Similar considerations apply if birds are attracted towards the point -
though in this case, you must be careful not to use a model for the
detection function that fits the artificial 'spike' at zero.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
> > with reference to my previous question dated 29/11/04 I was able to write a software to apply a methods described in chapter 4 (section 4.3) of the book Advanced distance sampling by Buckland et al.
> >
> > and that system seems working appropriately in the sense that the model predicts the distribution of radiocollared fallow deer in the area.
> >
> > However some doubts remain.
> >
> > 1. I've used 4 surveys to estimate local fallow deer density. To do that I used the ESW estimated by pooling the data of the 4 surveys and the waiting distance I used all points of the 4 surveys. By instance

> >
> > A------B-----A------------C (translated transect of fig 4.1)
> > x1.....x2...x3...........x4 coordinates
> >

> > I computed  l_i=x2-x1 between A and B, between B  and A (x3-x2) and so on where A,B,C are detection  points from the first, second,.. survey.
> >
> > I argued that the density obtained is the "average density" of the 4 surveys but I worry whether or I've to divide by 4 (or for some other value) to obtain it?

Yes, by pooling, you're increased the encounter rate fourfold, so you will
need to divide the density estimate by 4.

> > 2. Fallow deer occurs in clusters. For each point of the grid used to extrapolate the model, I used the following equations derived by eq. (4.1)
> >
> > D_hat=s_hat/2*mu_hat*l_hat
> >
> > where s_hat is the average cluster size per habitat (we detected no size bias). Is this correct or there are smarter way to modelise s_hat?

That should be fine.  You could also fit a spatial model for s - see p68
of the advanced distance sampling book.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: 2 questions
messages.body_plain:
I've been working forest bird point transect data (23 forest stands
[plots], 6 points per stand, 6 visits per point in 2 summers) and found
something odd.  I've imported the data and calculated densities and
detection probabilities for each of three silviculture treatments (Patch
cuts, thinned, and uncut).  Ok, fine.  Preliminary numbers look correct and
very reasonable.  For a few species we don't have sufficient detections in
one or 2 treatments (i.e. only 49 blue jays in patch cut plots).  So I went
through and analyzed all the data together for one density estimate across
all study sites for the species, which can be used to look at detection
probabilities per point between treatments, etc.  However, the density
estimate is essentially the sum of the densities for each treatment summed.

For example:
Blue Jays   Treatment   Density   N     Pa
              PATCH      0.024   49   0.4022
              THIN       0.062  101   0.2787
              UNCUT      0.030   66   0.3805
    All combined  0.115 216   0.3221

So the N is correct for all detections of the species and the Pa seems
reasonably in the middle of the highest and lowest Pa's, but the density
has got to be wrong.  Certainly this is incorrect, but we're not sure why.

We are not stratifying our data (not sure if we should), but we have
included a covariate of age (time since the site was harvested).  I was
suggested to open up the Model Definitions Properties page and on the
Estimate tab, look near the bottom of the page for the statement that
reads, "Global density estimate is a ____ of stratum estimates."  I have it
saying "mean" rather than "sum", but since we're not stratifying the data
it makes no difference.  I've played around with different options of sum
and mean, but it makes no difference.

On the topic of covariates, we also have variables such as PC1 and PC2 for
veg structure, observer, and visit (early May, late May/early June, and mid-
June), but haven't incuded them as we're not sure how and/or what's most
appropriate.

Any ideas on either topic?

Thanks,
   Scott

messages.subject: Re: 2 questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Scott,
(answer going also to the list, thanks to Scott for a previous e-mail=20
clarifying a few points)

I believe that the problem with D's not "adding up" is the following: =20
when you filter the data by treatment, you only filter observations=20
(i.e. detections), but you do not filter the effort (i.e. number of=20
points). So the density estimates for the treatments are underestimated,=20
because you (on average, assuming that a similar number of points was=20
used in each treatment) have 3 times more effort than the real one for=20
the treatments. The global density estimate should be fine, provided you=20
have equal coverage in each treatment, but since you are interested in=20
treatment specific densities, you need to change the way you are doing=20
the analysis.

To get a density by treatment, maybe the best option is to modify the=20
distance projects to include treatment as a strata - then, in each=20
strata the adequate effort will be considered. For your global density=20
estimate, you should select "Global density is a mean of stratum=20
estimates, weighted by total effort in strata". Then you can estimate=20
density by strata and, if sample size is small, estimate a pooled=20
detection function across strata. Note however that in such case=20
comparing estimated densities or the encounter rates is the same, as the=20
probability of detection is the same for the 3 treatments. An=20
alternative would be  including treatment as a covariate instead of=20
using it as a stratum - this might allow you to estimate detection by=20
strata with a relatively small sample size by strata.

Notice that if you estimate separate detection functions by treatment=20
(large sample size), then treatment estimates should be independent and=20
comparisons are straightforward. However, if you use a pooled detection=20
function (with or without covariates), then care must be taken because=20
the estimates in each stratum(=3Dtreatment) are not independent.

For the comparisons to be meaningful, you need to be careful with how=20
you estimate variances. You say you have 3 treatments, over 23 forest=20
plots (I assume each plot has only one treatment), 6 points per stand, 6=20
visits per point and 2 summers. The easy way to proceed is to pool all=20
the detections coming from each point, as a single "big-point", and=20
record the point  effort as the number of times the point was visited=20
(e.g. say effort =3D 6*2=3D 12). This is important because you cannot tre=
at=20
each of these visits to the same points as independent. If your stands=20
are separated in space, yet points in a stand are closer together, then=20
the points in a given stand cannot be considered independent either; you=20
should consider pooling all the observations at a stand as a "big-point"=20
(in this case, effort would be =3D 6*6*2=3D 72).

If you think that some of the covariates you have available are=20
responsible for changes in detection (as it is, it seems that the one=20
you use, "time since the site was harvested" is a good candidate), you=20
might want to include these and the estimate density in each stratum=20
(the probability of detection is then estimated conditional on the=20
observed covariate values on each stratum). This should reduce the=20
variance estimates and hence, given that a treatment effect exists, it=20
should be easier to detect.

Hope this helps, other comments welcome.

Tiago
